title: Lock a monitor with a keyed cable lock: T-bar into its 3 x 7 mm slot, held home while the key turns, key out
instruction: Lock the monitor with the cable lock and take the key out.
context: Offices, schools, libraries and shops lock their monitors and laptops to the desk with a keyed cable lock. The lock's T-bar must go square into a 3 x 7 mm slot on the monitor's back, and the head must stay pressed flat on the monitor while the key turns a quarter turn: only then does the T-bar turn crosswise behind the slot's wall. If the head backs off, the bar binds in the slot or turns outside it and the lock comes straight out. The steel cable's weight and stiffness tip an unheld head out of square, so one hand holds the head home while the other turns the key and pulls it out. The monitor stands free on the desk.
setup: Positions in m from the midpoint between the arm bases, on the table top (x forward, y left). Dell E2422H 23.8 in monitor (black, 3.9 kg with stand), screen toward a user's seat on the desk's far side, so the robot works at its back; not clamped: panel 552.6 x 331.6 x 49.7 mm, lower edge 88.7 mm up, no tilt; centre line y -0.07; rear housing back at x 0.42; stand base 222 x 171 mm, x 0.30-0.47, taped. Security slot (7 x 3 mm, long side level) at (0.42, 0.045), 134 mm up. Kensington MicroSaver 2.0 lock (K65020WW): 10 mm nose, 18 mm barrel, 34 mm long; T-bar 2.2-4 mm out; tubular key in, unlocked, bow 22 x 22 x 3 mm. Lies near (0.24, -0.02), T-bar to the monitor, bow flat (LOCK_SEED: up to 2 cm, 20 degrees). Its 5 mm steel cable runs 0.6 m on the desk, bowing toward the robot, to a Kensington Desk Mount Cable Anchor (K64613WW) at (0.30, 0.50) where it is tied; beyond, it loops round the desk leg. Arms in the ready pose.
scoring: 0 (latched) if at any time the monitor slides over 3 cm, tips over 10 degrees or leaves the desk (tape marks, video). Else at the end: 1.0 locked (head flush on the monitor, T-bar through the slot and turned crosswise), key out of the lock, both grippers 4 cm or more from the head, held 2 s; 0.8 the same with a gripper still at the head; 0.6 locked with the key in; 0.3 T-bar through the slot, head flush, not turned; 0.1 the T-bar went through the slot at some point but is out at the end; else 0 (a key turned with the head outside the slot scores 0). Real trial: locked = the head stays in under a 20 N straight pull with a luggage scale after the trial and no 1 mm gap at the nose (1 mm card); key out and gripper clearance from the video.
reset_notes: Nothing is used up. Unlock with the key (or the second key), take the head out, put the key in the head in the unlocked position and lay the lock on its tape marks, T-bar toward the monitor, bow flat. Put the monitor back on its base tape marks if it moved.
fidelity: Approximate. Rigid boxes: head, T-bar (estimated 6.0 x 2.2 mm crossbar) and pins in a 7 x 3 mm slot, 0.4-0.6 mm clearance; contact alone decides insertion, binding and holding. The key is its own body on a joint: it turns the T-bar and comes out only when locked, under 3 N. Detents are a weak spring. The 0.6 m of cable to the anchor is 12 hinged 50 mm segments with an estimated bending spring; the coiled rest is not simulated. The monitor is one rigid body.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0; scripted demo: 1.0 (seed 0; also 1.0 on seeds 4 and 10)
